Mr. Speaker, this bill is the
outcome of certain representations made by the late Judge Sedgewick, the chairman of the dominion trade and industry commission. It includes certain provisions which he regarded as desirable in the public interest and which were omitted from the original bill. I may say that the bill was drafted by the late chairman himself. The purpose of the legislation is to make it possible to establish standards in respect of commodities which are not now provided for by any existing act of parliament, and also to prescribe the words by which the material content of any commodity shall be represented. A number of acts, such as the Food and Drugs Act, the Canada Grain Act, the Meat and Canned Foods Act, the Inspection and Sale Act, et cetera, provide for standards in respect of certain commodities, but there are many commodities which cannot be made subject to standards under any existing legislation. subtopic: USE OF NAME "THE PRESBYTERIAN CHURCH IN CANADA"

speechtext:
Hon. W. R. MOTHERWELL (Melville) moved for leave to introduce Bill No. 57, respecting the United Church of Canada.
He said: This bill comes to us from the senate, and is founded upon a mutual agreement associated with reciprocal good fellowship between the official representatives of ihe United Church of Canada and corresponding representatives of that body of Presbyterians who decided to remain out of church union, as to the use of that official designation "The Presbyterian Church in Canada."
Inasmuch as both parties to this difference make some conscientious claims to some form of continuity, it was unanimously agreed, after friendly discussions, that that portion of the Presbyterian church which remained out of union, should have accorded to it the right by law to use the official term "The Presbyterian Church in Canada," without prejudice in any way to the rights, status, or powers of the United Church of Canada. This bill is designed to give effect to that reciprocal understanding.
I therefore take much pleasure in moving the first reading of this bill, seconded by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Stewart).
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: On the orders of the day :

subtopic: REFUSAL OF CREDIT AND LOANS BY BANKS TO SASKATCHEWAN MUNICIPALITIES
speechtext:
I wish to direct to the Minister of Finance a question based on a number of reports I have received from municipalities in Saskatchewan, and particularly a letter I have received today from the reeve and secretary of one municipality. The letter is to the effect that the municipality has been refused lines of credit and further loans from the banks on the excuse that the dominion government's guarantee for the purchase of seed and feed last spring has not been carried out. The question is: Will the minister say whether the banks are right in stating as a proper excuse for not extending loans, that the guarantee has not been carried out?
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): I would have preferred notice of the question because it might involve something which is not within my immediate present knowledge, but I am quite sure that the dominion has in every respect followed through with the obligation of the guarantee authorized by this house one year ago. I am quite sure there must be some misunderstanding on the part of some branch bank involving a statement of that sort. As to whether the guarantee for specific amounts has yet been executed, that is another matter, because, of course, specific amounts could not be guaranteed until they were definitely ascertained from all municipalities for every bank. But there is no doubt in the mind of any of the banks, I am quite sure, as to the obligation of the dominion with respect to its guarantee given one year ago.

The house in committee of ways and means, Mr. Sanderson, in the chair.
On schedule I:
Customs tariff-438a. Automobiles and motor vehicles of all kinds, n.o.p.; electric trackless trolley buses; chassis for all the foregoing, 17i per cent.
Provided, that machines or other articles mounted on the foregoing, or attached thereto for purposes other than loading or unloading the vehicle, shall be valued separately and duty assessed under the tariff items regularly applicable thereto.

We had an important discussion on this item just before six o'clock yesterday. The question merits more consideration than it has so far received. We are all interested to know whether statements made in the chamber yesterday with respect to certain industries threatening to leave the country are correct or otherwise. Some hon. members have stated that one of the industries has decided to leave Canada. On the other hand the Minister of Finance said he was not aware of anything of that kind having occurred.
Hon. CHARLES A. DUNNING (Minister of Finance): My hon. friend is not reading my statement when he says that. The allegation in the newspaper article, which the leader of the opposition (Mr. Manion) read yesterday, was that two of the large automobile manufacturers were contemplating leaving Canada, and my reply had reference to that statement. To-day I can confirm my reply, that I have no knowledge, and the government has no knowledge whatsoever, that any of the large automobile manufacturers are contemplating closing their Canadian plants.

Is it true, then, that any of the smaller ones are closing their factories on account of the removal of this three per cent excise duty?
Mr, DUNNING: We have no notification that any are definitely closing.

Well, we had better have that statement from the minister. The question is an important one. My mind goes back to 1926, when certain reductions were made in the automobile duties under the late Mr. Robb's budget. When these reductions were announced the automobile factories closed down almost entirely, and a few days later they organized a tremendous demonstration right here in Ottawa. Many thousands of employees came here and protested against the reduction. But when no action was taken by the government the factories reopened, and I believe that the following year they did

Canada-United, States Trade Agreement
more business than ever before in the history of the industry in Canada. In Oshawa, particularly was that true. Whether that was due to the reduction of the duty I cannot say, but the fact is although this tremendous protest was made, when the government took no action the matter blew over and the industry went on as actively as before.
I do not know what the position is now, whether they are just carrying on an agitation as they did in 1926, trying to induce the government to restore the three per cent excise tax. If I am not mistaken, all the protection that is being removed at the present time from the automobile industry is the three per cent excise tax. If I am wrong in that, I hope I shall be corrected immediately. Under the 17J per cent duty the industry has been doing fairly well. Whether the three per cent excise now is of such vital importance to the industry I do not know. But it seems that whenever there is a reduction in duty affecting any particular industry we are bombarded with threats that if the duty is not restored the industry will be ruined. I do not take a great deal of stock in such arguments. There may be certain industries in respect of which even a three per cent difference in protection might have considerable effect, but I do not know whether the automobile industry is in that position. According to my knowledge, which is meagre, the disparity between prices of automobiles in Canada and the same machines in the United States is so great that I cannot see that a reduction of three per cent could make such a great difference to the manufacturers in Canada.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman to say he is opposed to the withdrawal of the three per cent excise tax?

I have offered no objection, because, so far as I can see, no case has been made out by the manufacturers to show that the industry would be seriously jeopardized. If I could be shown that the three per cent excise tax makes the difference between their remaining in business or closing down, I should certainly be opposed to removal of the tax. But all we have had is a number of statements and letters in general terms, nothing specific and definite. I object to these general statements which give us no clear knowledge of the situation.
Probably no hon. member of this house has taken a greater interest in the condition of the men and women employed in the industry than 'I have over a period of years. In 1926, when the duties were reduced, the
automobile industry was doing fairly well. It was doing fairly well in 1928, and employees who had come here to protest against the reduction in the tariff were the very ones who came about that time and protested against a reduction in wages. We all remember the strike in the automobile plants at Oshawa about 1928. At that time not half as many hon. members were prepared to take the part of the employees as supported the protest the year before.
I should like the minister to state if he can what the reduction of three per cent really means to the automobile industry. We have not had a clear statement from the manufacturers or from anyone else. This three per cent excise tax has been in effect, I believe, for six or seven years?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Since 1931.

A little over seven years. Prior to that time the manufacturers were doing fairly well. I cannot see why we should always be threatened with the closing down of an industry the moment a duty is reduced. When a duty goes up, no threats are made by manufacturers, no better conditions are provided for those employed in the industry, and no greater stability of employment results. The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) last night spoke of the condition of the employees of this industry in his city. We know it is not very good. Yet I think the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Moore) said their annual wages were the fourth highest in Canada. That may mean much or nothing. All we know is that the annual wages of those employed in the automobile industry are barely sufficient to give them a decent existence. To-day on account of improvement in industrial technique it takes a smaller number of days to produce the same number of automobiles than it did a few years ago. If that process continues we are bound to have a greater problem of unemployment to face as time goes on. No scheme of insurance or anything of the kind can take care of the part-time employee. I do not wish, however, to go into that aspect of the question now. But if it is possible to have a clear and concise statement from the minister as to what this three per cent really means, we should have it. We should not continually have these threats from the automobile manufacturers that unless the duty is kept up they will close their plants.

It was not my intention to say anything about this item until other hon. members made some observations. I congratulate this country upon having a government which is prepared to take part of the burden off the people in connection with this
2230	COMMONS
Canada-United States Trade Agreement
industry. I was a member of this house some years ago and am familiar with the occasion to which the hon. .member who has just sat down (Mr. Heaps) referred, when the tariff on automobiles was reduced in 1926 and we had a delegation which filled the lawn in front of the parliament buildings, consisting I believe of about 5,000 people. They had banners and all that sort of thing, and they made all kinds of threats to the people of this country and particularly to hon. members of this house as to what would be done if we dared reduce the tariff on automobiles. In fact the demonstration was so noisy that one might think the whole industry was on the verge of ruin, I remember one man in front of this building who was so violent that he put his fist as close to my face as it is safe for any man to do, and said that if we did not recognize the terrible condition to which this industry was to be brought he did not know what was going to happen.
What did we do? The tariff at that time was reduced from 35 per cent to 20 per cent on cars costing up to SI ,200 and to 27J per cent on the others. What was the result? Well, what are we hearing now? We are told that if we dare to remove even this excise tax, again the industry is going to close down, or at least some companies will have to move out of Canada. On the previous occasion no companies moved out of Canada; on the contrary they enlarged their plants, sold more cars, created more employment and the industry prospered more than it had prospered at any other time. The same thing will happen to-day. If we make it easier for people to purchase cars, more cars will be purchased.
This tariff schedule provides a rate of 17J per cent, but let us examine how that rate of duty is applied. We have three large companies manufacturing cars in this country, the Ford Motor Company, the Chrysler Corporation and General Motors. I ask this question: does any dealer in Canada who is associated with any of these companies purchase cars made in the United States? Can he purchase any cars made by these companies in the United States and bring them into Canada? The answer is that it cannot be done. In rare cases a man in Canada might sell a car to some customer who happened to be down in the United States, but that has to be done by special arrangement. Then I would ask the further question, against whom this tariff operates. Certainly it does not operate against these three major companies, which do the vast majority of the automobile business in Canada. The tariff is listed at 17J per cent, but as it is applied

at present there is an effective rate of duty to the consumers of Canada

and that is what matters-of between 28 and 29 per cent. I challenge anyone to deny that. Anyone who does so cannot know the facts.
Develop that.

It is not hard to develop. Not one automobile company in Canada will deny it. Some of the accountants employed in the automobile industry were in my office on several occasions, and they admitted this to be the case. When I purchase a car in the United States I must pay the duty of 17i per cent on the retail price of that car. A couple of years ago I bought in this country what I thought, and still think, was a very good car. There was a radio installed in it, and while I was in the United States the radio went out of commission. I stopped at the garage of a dealer handling the same kind of car, and immediately alongside my car on the street was a United States car of exactly the same type. On many occasions we in this house have been told .that the Canadian car contains a little better material, that it is a little more substantially made in order to meet Canadian conditions. We examined the two cars, which were also examined by the mechanics, and found that the materials were identical, and I believe the workmanship was just as good in the one case as in the other. But the retail price of that car in that city was $859, while the retail price of the same car in Saskatoon, where I live, was $1,260. The differential in freight as between that city in the United States and Saskatoon amounted to $100. In other words on a car which retailed in the United States at $859, after allowing for freight I was obliged to pay a difference of something over $300. That is a pretty serious matter.
What about the sales tax, as a matter of information?
I have forgotten the exact figures. There was a little difference, but it was very slight.
May I ask the hon. member if there will be any reduction when this schedule is passed?

Was that an automobile
manufacturing company?
It is one of the big companies.

Would the hon. member
mention the name?
It is the Ford Motor Company. Is that a big enough company for you?
All right-just for information.

Although I am not going
to discuss those items, I have been reading recently something of the set-up of the companies in the textile trade. I ask myself this question, and I put it to every hon. member: Are we being asked to give protection of an undue character to all these commodities in order that dividends may be paid on completely watered stock? If that kind of thing is to be permitted to continue it will be a serious condition for this country. The producers of western Canada who are trying to live will not be permitted to live unless wo have a reduction in the prices of commodities which they require in order that they may produce the commodities which they should produce.
I want to thank the government for taking off this three per cent. I want to ask them to go farther. I ask them to change the incidence of the collection of this tariff so that it will be on the retail price of the car in the United States, and so that the tariff rate will not be 17i per cent but will be cut down to 5 or 6 or 7 per cent. That will enable the consumer in this country to get his car at a more reasonable price than he ever got it before.
I had no notion whatever of saying anything about it, but when I hear hon. gentlemen berating the government for taking off the excise tax of three per cent, and when I find that outside of the house the automobile companies and the parts industry are making the same kind of fuss-well, to my mind,

Canada-United, States Trade Agreement
what is being done outside of this house is almost blackmail. I do not blame hon. members who receive these stories; they are reflecting that attitude. But in my humble judgment this automobile industry has had all the pap-feeding which any industry should ever have had. The sooner we get down to a better basis, the better it will be for the industry itself and for the consumers of Canada.

May we return for a moment to the original situation? We entered into negotiations with the United States for mutual benefit under a trade treaty. Our negotiators went down there, and an agreement was made about this three per cent excise tax. It is now suggested that this should be changed.
There are two alternatives open to us. One is that the negotiators should be sent back there, and that they should speak to that nice, fine, mild-voiced southern gentleman, Mr. Hull, and say, " We have two or three large United States corporations operating in Canada. We have lowered the excise tax against United States importations, and we suggest to you that you permit an amendment of this agreement so that the people of Canada may continue to exploit themselves for the benefit of two of your largest motor car companies." That is all it amounts to. These are two, strong United States companies-Canadian companies let me say, with United States stockholders-and that is the suggestion.
The other alternative, a somewhat different one, was embodied in the suggestion made yesterday by the Minister of National Revenue, when he said:
The suggestion made to me as Minister of National Revenue is that the law respecting valuations for duty purposes is not being properly applied by the Department of National Revenue.
The hon. gentleman's ears and heart are touched by the voice of pleading from the motor companies, and he thinks that something may be done.
All that I can say in that regard is that these representations are receiving the consideration of the Department of National Revenue at the present time. I do not think there is anything more I can add.
But may I point out this to the Minister of National Revenue. There are many far more deeply convinced protectionists who have occupied for years the position which he now occupies; and if these mighty gleaners have gone over the field seeking justification for alteration of valuations, how does my less strenuous friend think he can find it under present conditions?
Did I understand the hon. member to say that I thought some change should be made?

I will read the
paragraph.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: The hon. member interpolated something in the middle of it; that is scarcely fair.
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance will permit me to read the full paragraph before he suggests what has been interpolated into it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: But there was an interpolation.

Let me read the item:
But the suggestion that has been made to me as Minister of National Revenue-and that is probably the reason why my name is mentioned in that regard-is that the law respecting valuations for duty purposes is not being properly applied by the Department of National Revenue. All that I can say in that regard is that these representations are receiving the consideration of the Department of National Revenue at the present time. I do not think there is anything more I can add.
Yes.

Yes, that is what my hon. friend said. In other words, the suggestion is that they are making a very careful investigation to see if it may not be possible to adjust this situation.
May I say this to my hon. friend and to the House of Commons: Rather a hundred times I would have it that we should go boldly to the United States and ask for an amendment than that, having entered into negotiations with those people, who understood our system of valuation, we should then turn around and change that valuation at the request of interested parties. True, there is no limitation to genius in a corner seeking to satisfy the needs of greed. But I do say that we should hesitate, and hesitate a long time, before we face that method of settlement.
Let me turn to the next item. We had a story yesterday from the hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin):
I must say, and I say this in the house, that I first of all thank the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ilsley) for the statement he has made to-day, namely that this whole matter is receiving the consideration of the government. I want the committee to know that there could have been no more painstaking effort on the part of the Minister of Finance and on the part of the Minister of National Revenue in considering this problem, as they have done during the past two or three weeks particularly, in conference day after day with members from Essex county and other parts of Ontario and myself.

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
What is wrong with that?

Government by the
house; government by party; a democracy- or what have we?
Did the hon. member ever confer with me about these matters?
Yes, quite; but I did not have much of a conference, by the way.
Oh, oh.

But here is the situation: I point this out-my hon. friend admits it himself and I will prove it. In a speech he delivered last year to the junior chamber of commerce of Canada, in the Windsor Hotel, Montreal, he used these words:
Another feature of political public service of the "less pleasing" type is the continuous and at times intense pressure of special interests-sectional, corporate or individual. I have often said, and now repeat, that no government can be truly efficient unless it continuously places the general interest above the particular, the national above the sectional. But it is so hard to defend the general interest, when everyone is fighting for some special interest.
So I say the minister himself admits the condition which exists. Why should anyone else attempt to deny it?
I now come to another paragraph of the hon. member for Essex East:
In answer to the hon. member for St. Paul's (Mr. Ross) I referred to the provisions of the Customs Act. In my judgment there is within the terms of the present Customs Act an opportunity to obviate whatever harm may exist because of the removal of the three per cent excise.
What did the hon. member for Essex East mean by that sentence? He meant that within the four corners of the Customs Act there remains the power for the Minister of National Revenue to obviate or to nullify the change which had been made. All that I am pleading for to-day before this house is that if we are to change this, let us face the situation, let us admit that we are wrong; but do not change it now by a shifting of valuations when these valuations have remained fixed over a long period of years.
I ask this question. We have in Canada two or three large United States automobile manufacturing companies. We have gone through this list which I have before me, and it has not been suggested for one moment that we change the excise tax in regard to the other items; these were Canadian companies.

There is no reason except that the pressure upon this item is greater. And why the pressure? Pressure comes from power, and these gentlemen have the power.
I have before me the net earnings of the Ford Motor Company. In the year 1935 they were $2,109,000; 1936, S3,888,000; 1937, $4,-
375,000.	The record of their accumulated surplus has been as follows: 1935, $17,167,000; 1936, 818,825,000; 1937, $20,939,000,-almost $21,000,000-of accumulated surplus. I shall watch with some calmness and detachment the attitude which the government takes on this particular question. But I am quite confident what the attitude of the people of Canada will be if the government of to-day decides that by some other way rather than in the regular way they give back to this corporation and other similar corporations that which they took from them by negotiation.
We heard the other day some remarkable things which I think ought to be touched upon. My hon. friend the member for Ontario told us that the farmers had a very high tariff and that that tariff had done wonders for them. Well, that high farm tariff began in 1930. Liberals have always claimed that tariffs, so far as protecting the farmers are concerned, are hopeless, useless and absurd. Within three years <pf the inauguration of these farm tariffs the prices of farm products in this dominion were cut in two. What did the government do? The government of that day, in 1933, raised the tariffs still further. But something happened later. The price of farm products in the past year has declined twenty-five per cent. I ask you what would have happened among the industrial leaders, what would have happened among labour men, if in that year's time the price of their products had been cut 25 per cent? Suppose the price of automobiles had been cut by twenty-five per cent, let alone three per cent, would not everything possible have been done by parliament to put prices back? Suppose wages of labour had been by some means cut in two; would there not have been a desperate effort to restore them to the normal level? But although we are frankly unable to face the problem of the decline in farm prices, we stlil continue to hold up by every power we have, or as Mr. Bennett used to say, we exhaust the resources of civilization, to hold up the prices of manufactured goods.
There is one other thing which my distinguished friend from Ontario mentioned. He said that we should support this particular industry for another reason-that it is based on something we shall need in the future. The Minister of National Defence is here

Canada-United States Trade Agreement
and I put this to him: If we are going to vote money for a particular purpose in a democratic parliament, should we not vote it definitely for that purpose? If you suggest that we should maintain our automobile industry by artificial means because possibly it may be necessary to us for military reasons in later years, then by all means submit a measure such as that to the house and let us consider it seriously and bravely. But I suggest that the idea that we pay more for an automobile now with the happy idea that we will get it back years later with a tank thrown in, is as great a piece of folly as could possibly be conceived.
It is suggested that the farmers of western Canada should have no objection to this. Well, the farmers of Manitoba recently presented a brief before the dominion-provincial commission in which the estimate was made that in a normal year high tariff interests took from the farmers of western Canada the sum total of 847,000,000. And what do we pay to maintain the price of wheat? The sum of 848,000,000. I suggest to the Minister of Finance that it might be helpful to short-circuit the cheque which we send to the western farmers, pass it directly to the Canadian manufacturers, and let it go at that, thus saving the expense of the present roundabout way of doing it,
It is further suggested that having established this reciprocity treaty with the United States, we should now enter into negotiations with them over another thing-and I shall relate all this to automobiles.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Pretty far afield.

Not at all far afield, as you will see in a moment. It has been suggested that we enter into negotiations with the United States to permit them to increase the price of coal which they ship into this country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I must rise to a point of order, Mr. Chairman. If we are to have a general budget debate on this item of automobiles, my hon. friend is quite in order, but so will every hon. member be who follows him and attempts to expand in the same manner as he is now doing. I suggest to him in all seriousness that coal is not automobiles.

speechtext: I think the point of order raised by the Minister of Finance is well taken. I would ask the hon. member for Huron North to confine his remarks to the item under discussion, which is automobiles.

Speaking to the point of order, it is rather curious, Mr. Chairman;

I am dealing directly here with the threat of an increased price on coal by negotiation with the United States, which necessitates in the view of some people an increase in the duty on automobiles. The Minister of Finance does not recognize that fact, but it is true. It may seem that we have wandered far afield, but it is directly and positively connected with the point I was going to discuss-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would point out to the hon. member that I have given my ruling, and I would ask him to abide by it.

I accept your ruling, Mr. Chairman. Here is the point at issue. Are we going to negotiate directly with the United States, or are we going to change this rate by indirect action? The facts proving the critical situation brought about by the change in the tariff are as follows:
When a change in the Canadian content, from 50 to 40, was brought about in the latter part of 1938, the Packard Company of Canada were affected to the extent that the manufacturers decided to manufacture in Canada two jobs that had previously been imported, namely, the Super-eight and the convertible coupe.
Immediately after the announcement of the change in Canadian content, stock for these two jobs were brought into the Canadian plant in preparation for immediate production, but when the announcement of the excise tax being taken off, appeared in the papers, this stock was sent back to the American plant, and it was announced that these jobs would not be built in Canada.
Previous to the excise tax being taken off of imported automobiles, the company was seriously thinking of building or buying a larger plant, in order to increase production from 6 to possibly 30 or 40 jobs per day, which would include the new light-six which the company is putting on the market some time in July.
Now in addition to the super-eight and the convertible, they have also discontinued production of their model 120. Production on the 115, the only job now being built in Canada, will cease within the next ten days. The plans of the company after that date are rather indefinite. Rumour has it, that the plant will then close until possibly July 15, when there is a possibility that the company may start producing the new light-six. This is not definitely decided on as yet.
At six jobs per day the company employs approximately 80 men. If the increase in production had gone through, you can see what a difference it would have made in the economic situation of the border cities.
All cars discontinued in Canada are now being imported at the rate of about 20 or 25 per week.

No; we had one or two speeches the other day, and one to-day, from the Conservative party. That indicates that this question cuts directly across parties. It is one of those questions that are of greatest difficulty, inherent in the nature of this country itself. Every government has found difficulty with it, and I assume every government will for some time to come.
May I say at the outset that to answer specific questions, such as those asked by the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Heaps), would be difficult because he insists on asking about an automobile, whereas no one can answer a question with respect to an automobile unless he knows a number of other things-for instance, how many automobiles are produced in a particular year, in a particular plant. I mention that for this reason. If you had a Canadian tariff sufficiently high to enable the manufacturer of 1,000 automobiles a year to pay decent wages and a reasonably low interest on his investment, you would have a duty on a comparable car high enough to enable the so-called Big Three to make profits altogether out of reason. That is our difficulty. The hon. member for Essex East (Mr. Martin) told the committee quite properly that three small manufacturers had left Canada. He also told the committee that no one of these three left Canada in consequence of this treaty, because they were gone before the treaty was negotiated.
The annual production in Canada, which had been attained by at least two of the three concerns to which my hon. friend refers, could not possibly have enabled them to make money on their Canadian enterprise considered as a separate entity. One Ford car turned out in a plant would cost millions of dollars, but millions of Ford cars can be produced at a very few hundred dollars each. There is the nub of the problem so far as Canada is concerned.
I am under no apprehension whatever that either Ford, Chrysler or General Motors, who have made and are making between eighty and ninety per cent of the Canadian car production, will pull out of Canada, to use a common phrase. I go further and say I believe that those corporations, while they are controlled by foreign capital-

Two of them.

But even those that are
controlled by foreign capital have a sufficient sense of the value of their Canadian market, and their export markets from Canada, that they will not lightly take any arbitrary "pull* up stakes" attitude. I believe that the three great producers of automobiles will carry on. But I say to this committee as sincerely as I can, that I can see no way of erecting a tariff structure which will be fair to Canadian consumers and at the same time will allow profitable operation of a company which is going to make only a thousand or two thousand cars a year. It just cannot be done. Economy to the consumer is brought about by the production in one plant of a great number of standardized units.
Having said that, may I say I found something to agree with in what everyone has said on this subject, and also something to disagree with. anyone suggest that the ploughing back of earnings into industry for the creation of more capital goods which in turn produce more units of product is watered stock?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General

As to that opinions may differ, as to the extent to which the building up of the great Ford enterprise has been on account of tariff protection and the extent to which it is a result of mechanical genius allied to mass production and mass selling methods. For my part I do not believe it would ever have been possible to produce cars as cheap as they are at the present time if Henry Ford had not ploughed back the profits into that institution and thus build up its capital structure and its physical equipment to the point they have reached to-day. Watered stock, to my mind, is stock which is issued without having any real physical value back of it. I distinguish clearly between watered stock and the practice on which some of our great industries have been built up of ploughing back legitimate earnings into further physical plant and productive equipment.
As far as this item is concerned, anyone listening to the discussions in this house, no matter in what year, must realize how difficult the question is of balancing as far as possible the interest of producers and consumers of this very important facility in Canada. The government have done the best they could, in the light of the information which they had, in the proposal which is now before the committee. That proposal is to bind the duty, that it shall not increase during the term of the agreement; and tether, inasmuch as this is one of the items mentioned in the treaty, to undertake to propose to the Canadian House of Commons at a convenient opportunity after the passage of the treaty itself that the excise tax in connection with automobiles shall be repealed. I do not think I can add anything more. I believe that what are called the Big Three will continue to function in Canada to the fullest extent rendered possible by Canada's demand for motor cars and the opportunities for export from Canada, which are not by any means small. And I believe that the Canadian consumers will benefit.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT THE SENDING THROUGH THE MAILS OP COMMUNISTIC LITERATURE

speechtext: The house resumed from Tuesday, February 21, consideration of the motion of Mr. Wilfrid Lacroix (Quebec-Montmorency) for the second reading of Bill No. 4, to amend the Post Office Act.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROHIBIT THE SENDING THROUGH THE MAILS OP COMMUNISTIC LITERATURE
speechtext:
I rise to say a few words in support of this bill. It relates to liberty, and as we all know, abuse of liberty brings licence, and licence invites restraint. The spread of communism, as described by the mover of the bill, reveals an appalling situation. It is a menace to our civilization; it is a plague; it is the product of diseased minds; it is something destructive of the social order and our political and religious institutions; it conduces to revolution.
Communism is defined in the bill in a manner which is clearly understandable by any of the members of this house. Its effects are obvious. The other day the attorney general of Ontario announced, I am informed, that conditions are becoming so bad in this province that an investigation is to be started to discover the sources of this evil. I am told that in Toronto are at least forty so-called schools organized under this and that name, cluibs of one kind and another, groups which behind closed doors receive instructions, all leading to the same object, always with the same results in view. The sponsors of these schools not only talk to these people but also have newspapers published in different languages, disseminating their doctrine, distilling it drop by drop and sending it throughout the country, preparing people's minds for the evil day. When it will come we do not know. But this represents a constant effort to destroy the present order and bring in a new order of things.
In my province the Duplessis government enacted a statute which has been adversely appreciated and much criticized outside our boundaries. I have studied the comments of the various newspapers in the province of Quebec, and I find that criticism is very light; approval is general, and after two years the effects of this law are good. It may be proper to mention that the premier of Quebec himself is possibly too much mentioned in connection with this law. It is true that he was the father of it; but it was unanimously adopted by the Quebec legislature; both parties supported it, and in that house there are members of different creeds and races. English, Scotch, Irish, Hebrews, all joined hands. Quebec is the only province which
r. MacNiuoi.j
now has a second chamber. Its legislative council is composed of eighteen Liberals and six so-called Conservatives, or twenty-four in all. The twenty-four unanimously approved this law, notwithstanding their differences in politics, race and religion. So it is the law of the province; it represents the voice of our people. But the effect of this law is defeated when it comes to the press, because daily from Toronto there are pouring into the province of Quebec, and the rest of Canada for that matter, newspapers upholding the communist doctrine, threatening our institutions and everything which is dear to us.
What shall we do? It is evident that the postal regulations are not sufficient. They are not applied. This is not the fault of the minister or of his officials, possibly not the fault of the regulations, except that they do not go far enough. The law is not sufficiently clear. What was said by the mover of this bill warrants, to my mind, the conclusion that something should be done to give more powers under the law to the Postmaster General (Mr. McLarty). I do not want to discuss the legal opinion of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe). I bow to his wisdom. But statutes are always difficult to interpret. It is a privilege of lawyers to differ. Often judges do not agree. Courts are not always in agreement with each other. The Supreme Court of Canada and the privy council have often not seen eye to eye. I look at this regulation 205 of the Post Office Department, which states:
It is forbidden to post for delivery or transmission by or through the post any obscene or immoral book, pamphlet ... or other publication, matter or thing, of an indecent, immoral, seditious, disloyal or scurrilous character.
That is the regulation. That is as far as it goes. Does it cover the ordinary communist paper? The minister, as reported at page 1183 of Hansard said:
In short, anything that is subversive, seditious, that advocates the use of force for the purpose of bringing about any change in the government of Canada, is already prohibited under the regulations of the Post Office Department.
Quite so. We do not need these regulations when force is advocated. That is an offence under the general law of the land, under the criminal code. But these newspapers of which I speak do not advocate force. If one takes any number by itself, its contents are not subversive of society. The papers give their poison drop by drop. It is a series of small events leading to a conclusion. It is the construction of a building. They build

Post Office Act-Communistic Literature
stone by stone, piece by piece. No one newspaper can be condemned under these regulations. The only part of the post office law under which something can be done in so far as mailable matter is concerned is section 7, paragraph (d), which reads:
The Postmaster General may .	.	. make
regulations declaring what shall and what shall not be deemed to be mailable matter for the purposes of this act.
"Mailable matter." This does not refer to the contents, to the ideas, to the writings themselves. It relates to the outside, because the section continues:
. . . and for restricting within reasonable limits the weight and dimensions of letters and packets and other articles sent by post.
But the section does not stop there. Year after year, according to needs, changes have been made by means of additions, and we find, always under the same paragraph (d) of section 7, that the Postmaster General may prohibit the sending of matter of an obscene or immoral nature. That is one clause. It does not cover the case of a communist newspaper. The next is prohibitive of matter which would "tend to injuriously affect the commercial or social standing of the persons" to whom it is sent. That is another addition. If it is not expressed in explicit terms, no regulation of the postal department can cover this case. The third addition has to do with illegal lotteries; the fourth deals with devices for the purpose of obtaining money under false pretences. Those four points are included in order to give additional powers to the Postmaster General. It is clear to me that the law officer who prepared this bill, in making his notes, grasped the point, because he says:
The purpose of this -amendment is to enlarge the powers of the Postmaster General as to the making of regulations. At present, the Postmaster General may prohibit -the sending of obscene or immoral publications. It is intended in this bill that he should also have the power to prohibit and prevent the sending of communistic literature.
That is the request, and I submit with all due respect that it should be granted. This is a necessary bill. It merely gives power to the Postmaster General to prohibit the sending of communistic literature. If, in the judgment of the Postmaster General or of the government, it is not necessary or judicious that there should be any regulation it need not be adopted. I say, however, that a move should be made in the direction proposed in this bill. Detection is out of the
question. The bill will not entail any particular labour or expense. It merely creates an offence which in course of time may be detected.
These remarks are offered in good faith for the consideration of the house, and I trust that the bill will receive favourable consideration. We speak of national unity, we speak of the flag, we speak of our heritage, we resort to arms to defend our borders. Let us start to-day to defend the hearts and minds of our people. This communistic doctrine has no right to exist under the Canadian flag; it has no right to be protected by the institutions of our country.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. S. WOODSWORTH (Winnipeg North Centre):

I think the last speaker (Mr. Gariepy) has given us one of the strongest reasons why this bill should be defeated. He says that the law as it now stands helps to defeat the purpose of the padlock law of Quebec. I have again and again spoken in this house against that padlock act. I believe it is depriving the people of the province of Quebec of their freedom. I believe it is an invasion of the field which, under the British North America Act, has been left to this parliament, that is the field of criminal jurisdiction, and for that reason alone I would be bound to protest and to vote against the bill before the house.
To those who have been in this house for any length of time I do not need to say that I am not a communist. The group I represent have a philosophy that is somewhat different from that of either the Liberal or the Conservative party, but it certainly is not the philosophy of the communist party. At the same time I think it right that we in this country should preserve the liberties of every section of the people of Canada. If the communist party commit any overt act, of course the law should be invoked, and they should be punished. But if it is just a matter of opinion, then they have just as much right to their views as anyone else. That has been my understanding of British free speech. They should have perfect liberty to propagate their ideas so long as those ideas do not lead to subversive acts.
Surely we have gone far enough now in the history of modern communism -to get away from the idea that everything done in the name of communism is necessarily wrong. Russia is a well-established country, and according to recent information Great Britain and France are likely to enter into some sort of defensive alliance with her. At any rate, you cannot sweep away a great population and an established order such as exists in

Russia. They have accomplished a great deal in that great country. I do not like their authoritarian principles at all; in fact, I am inclined to think the later rulers of Russia have rather betrayed the idealistic principles advocated at the beginning of the revolution. I do not like bringing about reforms by physical revolution, but I am not dealing with that question to-night. I do say, however, that no one can lightly pass over the achievements of any one great nation.
But, further than that, we have the communist party of Canada, an existing institution, taking part in various types of activity. I do not like the communist party. They have given our Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party more trouble than any other party.

Yes, almost as much. I have been opposed by the communist party and so have my colleagues. We differ in our points of view. But I must recognize that we have several communist members in our city councils. In my own province of Manitoba there is a communist member of the provincial house. There is a newspaper that comes into this house-one is put in my mail box-called The Clarion. Very often I do not agree with what I find in it; but it comes in, and I do not think it can be said -to be subversive in character. I understand that a representative of this communist paper has his place in our own press gallery.
So long as the communists confine themselves to advocating certain doctrines, but keeping within the law, I do not think we have any right to attempt to muzzle them.
I frankly admit that from the purely political' point of view I wish they were all back in Russia; it would be a great deal easier for us. But, as a matter of fact, a great many of them have not come from Russia; some are Canadian-born. They have adopted a particular philosophy; and, I repeat, so long as they keep within the law, they ought to have the full rights of citizenship.
There is one other point. Once we begin to adopt any authoritarian methods in Canada, we do not know where they will end. Already in the - province of Quebec certain people in high authority have classed the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation in the same group as the communists. These people have been quite misinformed; nevertheless it might readily mean that somebody might propose that the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation should not rent halls in the province of Quebec, or should not
[Mr. Woodsworth.J
circulate newspapers in the province of Quebec, or should not be permitted to do this, that or the other thing-in effect, was an illegal organization. What would be the outcome if we allowed arbitrary decisions of that kind?
It is much more in harmony with what most of us have been taught are the fundamentals of British liberty and the British constitution, if we allow people opportunities for free discussion. I for one believe that in the long run truth will win out. I believe that in the long run the doctrines of the communists will be shown to be false and ill founded, and that the truer doctrines, the better founded doctrines, will prevail.
It is an easy thing to get rid of a nuisance by shoving it to one side; it is an easy thing for the people of the province of Quebec to neglect the great social reforms, which neglect is really the basis of the communist agitation. If our social order is such that the people of Canada have opportunity for a decent living, they will not be appealed to by people who urge them to fight against that social order. I am a parliamentarian, because I believe that whatever reforms are necessary may be brought about by an intelligent electorate through constitutional means. If there is any attempt to stir up rebellion in this country, there are means by which that can be checked, but in the meantime I for one stand for full freedom of speech, and this house, if it is thoroughly British in its spirit, ought to stand for full freedom of speech.

Know the communists; learn about them, but under no circumstances fear them, because they have not the "intestinal fortitude" to interfere with the British system of justice. As long as you have par-liamentarianism and the right to speak in this house and say those things which you honestly believe, you need not be afraid of communism.
Let me relate something by way of diversion and interest, which will drive the point well home. I went to England in 1937. In journeying round the country, making an effort to learn what the working man thought about conditions, I slept in sixty different beds in eighty-six days. So that was some travelling. And if I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that for bed and breakfast I paid all the way from two shillings to eighteen shillings, you will know that I took in a long line and a pretty thorough one. I found myself in London in the first week of September, and the thought struck me:	This is Sunday in the
first week of September, 1937; in 1907 on Sunday in the first week of September I was in London also, and following my usual custom I went down to see how the poor people lived. In 1907 I wended my way to Petticoat lane, Middlesex street, a short street off Whitechapel in the east end of London. If you can visualize a narrow street with dingy houses and costers' barrows extending all the way up on either side of the pavement you will get a fair idea of what was happening on this Sunday morning; these itinerant vendors were selling second-hand goods of every kind. Policemen went three together up the centre of the street, afraid to go singly along the sidewalks for fear they would be battered from the open doors. The street was filled with tattered and bedraggled individuals, and poverty was everywhere. It was a common saying that you would have your watch stolen from you in Whitechapel and you could buy it back from the top barrow after you had passed through Middlesex street. Everywhere you saw individuals slowly recovering from the effects of the debauch of the night before.	,
So, thinking I might get a real view of the change in social conditions in England in
thirty years, I decided to do the same thing that Sunday in the first week of September, 1937. I went down to Middlesex street. The change amazed me. Young men and young women were well dressed and clean. The only dirty, tattered individual I saw was over fifty years of age. As I walked along the street they made a path for me. About one hundred yards up the street in a recess from the building line there was a cart, and on the cart a swarthy looking individual with shock, black hair yelling into a " mike." As I listened, the sound came imperfectly, because he did not know how to use a microphone properly, but he was talking communism. So I thought, now I will get a real slant on what is going on. The police officer on duty, the only one I could see, came down with his duty cuff on his arm and I accosted him.
I said: " Officer, do you allow this kind of thing to go on?" Well, he looked down at me-he was a big fellow-and said, " I don't think he is creating any disturbance." " Well,"
I said, " don't the people here make any noise about this, do they not complain about the disturbance? This is Sunday morning and they ought to have some rest." " Oh," he said, " look at them, they have their windows open, they are all listening to it." "But, officer,"
I said, " do you know what he is saying?" Then, with a tolerant smile he turned to me and said, " Oh, yes, sir, he is preaching communism; but you know this is a free country, sir, we have free speech here." I was compelled to say, " Thank God for that." If we can do the same thing in Canada; if we can face every overt idea; if we can challenge every opinion, maintaining our own while giving every other man the right to maintain his as long as he remains within the laws of our country, Canada will progress. But if we apply the hand that stultifies the imagination and destroys free opinion and free voice, God help Canada.

Whom does the hon. member mean by the members of the Conservative party in Ontario?
Those coming from Ontario. They are continually pointing to the fact that they are making such great contributions.
No, but we object to your criticism.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Shall the item carry?
I rise to another point of order. I think this committee should object to the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) taking the seat of the leader of the opposition.
I gave it to him. It is not a very nice seat anyway. I shall not be here long; I shall be over there.
We have that all fixed.

There is no hon. member who has greater sympathy with the west than I have. We should all act as Canadians, not criticize one part of the country from another part but all try to do our share.
Now a word for the miners. Section 89 of the Income War Tax Act exempts new producing mines from profit tax for a limited period after they come into production. A number of these new mines have been developed and brought to production by older mining companies. Section 4, paragraph (n) of the Income War Tax Act amendment of 1936 provides for exemption from income tax of dividends paid to an incorporated company by a company incorporated in Canada, the profits of which have been taxed under this act. But no exemption is given to the company receiving dividends from another company where the profits of that other company have not been taxed. In other words, the older mining companies that take the risk of developing new mining projects do not get the advantage of the exemption from taxation given to the new companies during the period in which the new companies are free from taxation under section 89. It seems to me that a simple amendment to section 4, paragraph (n) would cure the matter, and I suggest that that paragraph be amended by inserting, after the word "act" in the third line thereof the following words: "or by a company to which section 89 of this act applies during the period of such application."

I am familiar with the subject matter of that suggestion, and I hope the hon. member has made it or will make it in writing to the Minister of Finance, who must take the responsibility for that type of legislation. It should be discussed prior to the presentation of the budget. Possibly the Minister of Finance will see his way clear to accept the suggestion. But this is not the occasion to discuss it.

Well I shall do that, and perhaps the Minister of Finance will read Hansard.
I want to bring to the attention of the committee an interesting example of the taxation paid by an industry. I have altered these figures slightly, but they are all in proportion. Here is a company which pays $1,000,000 in wages in a year. In taxes it pays $175,000 a year. That is to say, for every $100 paid to the workers it pays $17.50 in taxes, or for every $25 a week paid in wages it pays $4.37 in taxes.

What taxes?
2274	COMMONS
Supply-National Revenue-Income Tax

All taxes, excluding customs and excise taxes. The dominion taxes alone paid by this concern were $146,500. I put this on record to show the very high taxes that industry has to pay, and meet the competition of other countries.
The amount of its taxes might be on account of the fact that it was making very high profits.
No, they are making very little profit. I have not the amount, but it is very low.
They must have made about a million dollars profit.
That amount of taxes would include municipal taxes, and provincial taxes and everything.
And sales tax.
Income tax has been collected in Canada, I think, for about twenty yearn, and in Great Britain for something like eighty or ninety years.
It has been continuously collected in Great Britain since 1842, but William Pitt the younger had an income tax in 1799.

Then it has been collected continuously in England for nearly one hundred years. We do not hear as much criticism to-day as we did ten or fifteen years ago, very likely from uninformed people, who objected to paying income tax unless they were perfectly certain that their neighbour, their friend and their acquaintance also paid it. Of course the tightening up process has gone on in this country until possibly there are very few evasions to-day. One of the reasons why the income tax in Great Britain has been accepted as it has, and why it is being accepted in an improved manner year after year in Canada, is because of its secrecy. To what extent does that secrecy exist. Is it absolute? Can anybody get information from the income tax branch of the minister's department for any purpose? Can provincial governments get any information, and can even the minister himself open the files of individuals and look through them?
Yes, the minister can, but I cannot remember doing it in the case of any individual. We do give some information to the provincial government.
Information of what kind?

The cases are limited to those covered by agreements made under statute. There is a provision in the income tax act

which enables us to enter into agreements with provinces for the collection of their income tax, and to give them certain information. To be absolutely accurate I would require to have the clauses of those agreements before me, but I can tell the hon. member the substance of the provision. It is that if the provincial government represents that in its opinion fraud exists in the returns made by those giving it information in respect of its laws, for example in connection with succession duties, then we agree to allow it access, at its request, to certain income tax returns, in order to enable it to enforce its laws.
They do not ask certain questions which are answered; they have access to the return of the individual?

If the attorney general, or in some instances the provincial secretary, or some responsible minister of the government of the province with which we have an agreement, will state that there are indications that there has been fraud, and will request access to the files, we allow them to be seen. Generally speaking that is the arrangement which exists. As I say, to put it quite accurately I should have the clauses before me.
For instance, can the provincial secretary of British Columbia ask for a copy of an individual return?
No, we have no agreement with British Columbia.
Then how is it done in practice? Is an accountant sent from Victoria to Ottawa?
I do not think we have given the government of British Columbia any information. We do not have any agreement with that province; we do not collect their income tax for them.

So the arrangement
exists only between certain provinces and the dominion government?

Yes, only those with which
we have agreements.

Some months ago, I cannot recall exactly but my recollection is that it was last summer, a question came up that, I believe, caused a good deal of irritation. It concerned the mining fraternity and was dealt with particularly by the Northern Miner, that mining journal of northern Ontario. I believe it had to do with section 37 (b)-

Section 32 (b).

Supply-National Revenue-Income Tax

I was familiar with it at
the time, and I remember that they had the impression that the mining fraternity, through legislation passed last year, were going to be unfairly treated in some of their company dealings. Has that matter been entirely straightened out to the satisfaction of both the government and the mining fraternity, because there was a good deal of complaint about it at the time and then the complaint ceased. I have been curious to learn what really happened, and I wonder if the minister would make a statement in this connection.
I think the matter has been straightened out to the satisfaction of both the mining interests and the government.

Would the minister explain briefly?
Mr. ILSLEA': Yes. The amendment passed at the end of last session preserved the principle that capital gains were not to be taxed, but the Northern Miner became alarmed. They thought we were introducing into our system the principle of taxation of capital gains. Capital gains are taxed in the United States; they are not taxed in Great Britain or in Canada. There are a great many legal decisions as to what constitutes capital gains and what constitutes profit or income. The amendment was designed to meet an abuse. We were not introducing any new practice; we were legalizing a practice that already existed, as to the legality of which some doubt had arisen. It was not confined to mining companies in terms; mines were not mentioned at all, but the main application was to companies engaged in prospecting.
Was it also in connection with recapitalization?

Yes, it did have some application there. Let us say a group decide to prospect for gold, with the intention not of mining the gold but of finding whether or not the gold is there and then selling their claim to a company that will develop and operate it. If it is clear under the law that their sole source of income is the increase in the value of the property they buy, they are regarded as primarily a trading company; they are not making their income in any other, way than selling at a high price what they acquire at a lower price. Under those conditions the gain is not regarded as, and is not legally, a capital gain. It is in fact the income of that syndicate, and is taxable. Then, instead of selling that property it may be possible for them to exchange it for shares and to divide the shares among themselves, or something of that kind.
They may get a million shares out of a three million share company.

Yes, and that is all the profit they make. The practice of the income tax division had been to value the shares they divided among themselves and say that was the profit they made. This section simply said that could be done, that the minister could put a value on shares that were divided in specie among shareholders or among the members of a group, and in that way the profit or income could be ascertained. But it was specifically provided in the section that it did not render taxable anything that was not legally income. It did not make a capital gain taxable. In some instances it might be a capital gain; the line is hard to draw. But it did not change that principle at all. It simply prevented what we regarded as a division in specie of property among shareholders in such a way that the gain could not be located or ascertained, that one could not find out what to tax.
Was any change made ultimately? Did the amendment that was put into force make any change, or is the law to-day exactly where it was before the amendment was passed by the house?

It may have been that before the amendment was passed the minister did not have the power to value shares. It certainly made that change; the minister now can value them. I do not know exactly what the effect was. If I remember correctly, I think the point was raised, and the question was whether there was any power to place a value on them?
At any rate it is settled at the present time to the satisfaction of both parties?
I would say so, as satisfactorily as anything ever is settled. There is no complaint about the section now, that I know of.
Because it is probably carried out exactly as it was before.
That is right.

Is it not mostly a matter of administration? There has been no change made in the amendment, and I would understand that it is only a matter of departmental ruling and administration. There has been no change in that.
No.

I have in mind
one man who had actually lost some $50,000 or $60,000, but who received an assessment
2276	COMMONS
Supply-National Revenue-Income Tax
notice for $3,000. Probably the minister knows about the case. It seems to me that it is a matter of administration and departmental ruling.

No; the whole trouble arose over a misunderstanding of the amendment. It was feared by a great many persons that we were trying to assess capital gains. When it became apparent that we were not doing anything but what we had been doing, and that we were putting the law in such a position that there was no question as to our right to do it, that we had been taxing income in the past and were continuing to tax it, but so as to prevent distribution of shares in this way without a value being put upon them, or with a nominal value put upon them, the minister was authorized to put a fair value upon them, so that the profit could be definitely ascertained, and the taxpayer assessed. It has been carried out fairly, as it was before, and the people have ceased to be afraid.

The minister has stated
that the remittance tax comes under this item. I have spoken about that tax on one or two occasions. As hon. members know, by that remittance tax five per cent is to be paid on all remittances from dividends, royalties, interest, rentals or any other investment. But under the 1936 amendment to the act, for some reason remittance taxes on films were reduced from five per cent to two per cent.
I suppose the minister has good reasons, of which we have not been informed, for that change. But the fact remains that there seems to be a general inclination towards gratuities to the picture producing companies in the United States. One excuse offered is that the films, after having had their run in Canada, are practically useless. Another reason given is that the remittances for the rentals of these films are not profits, but are really portions of the cost of the production in the United States.
I should like hon. members to realize that the saving by reason of this exemption applies only to the large picture producers in the United States. Nobody in Canada is benefited. I take the report of the Minister of Trade and Commerce for 1937, and there I find the rentals for those films. It must be remembered that the films are not brought into Canada as positives, to any great extent. A negative comes in and from that negative several prints are made in the processing plant at Montreal. The total tax paid to the government by reason of bringing in the negatives is about $90,000. But according to the Department of
rMr. Ilsley.]
Trade and Commerce, during the year 1937 the films have yielded to the film agency about $8,700,000. From that sum there was deducted for wages payable to the employees of some sixty-three film agencies in Canada the sum of $1,062,900. Then there was reserved from the $8,700,000 about thirty-five per cent to cover expenses and profits of the local film agencies. The fact remains that each year there is remitted between $4,000,000 and $5,000,000 to the picture producers of other countries.
I would ask the minister if he does not think in these strenuous days, when it is so difficult to balance the budget, and there are so many demands upon the Minister of Finance, he might give serious thought to repealing that section of the act, because it means a loss of about $150,000 a year to the taxpayers of Canada. If there is any good reason under the sun for such generosity or liberality to the picture producers in the United States the public would be interested to know about it. As I have said on previous occasions, no matter how small the investment in Canada of a resident of the United States may be, he suffers a loss of five per cent.
The claim is made that these remittances are really not dividends but they are a portion of the cost of production of the picture. Well, if a person makes an investment in Canada he certainly is contributing to the cost of production of a house, or whatever the investment may be, until he has recovered his investment. I think there is ground for considerable thought on the part of the minister and the government in reconsidering this exemption on films because it benefits only the picture producers in the United States.

I shall bring the remarks
of my hon. friend to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Dunning). I am very much interested in what he has said. He has spoken to me about the matter before, and he raised the point last year. It is not something that concerns me as Minister of National Revenue; it is a matter for the attention of the Minister of Finance. I shall be glad to discuss the matter with him and see that full consideration is given to the suggestion of the hon. gentleman.

Could the minister
give the total amount paid to his department last year by the gold mining interests of this country?

That is not segregated, but
it could be obtained.

I was trying to obtain
some idea of the revenue received from the

Supply-National Revenue-Income Tax
mining of precious metals in view of the services that we render. Perhaps at some other time I could ask this question.

I am not complaining
about income tax because I think it is the fairest tax we have in Canada, although I believe we think more of what we pay than of what we have left. If Ontario paid
S69.000.000 she must have $200,000,000 left, which is not too bad. Could the minister tell when it is possible for a business to obtain a clearance in connection with income tax? In other words, if you are buying or selling a business how far must you go back before you can get a clearance?

The matter can be settled
within a reasonable time. There is no fixed time, but if a company desires to settle up with the income tax division it can do so and the matter is not reopened unless fraud is discovered. There is no clearance possible that fraud will not reopen, but apart from that I am informed there is no trouble.

Could one obtain a
clearance for 1937 which could not be opened up unless fraud were discovered?
If a company is being wound up-

Not where a company is being wound up, but where an estate has to be settled. When would one know if one was going to be clear? I understand that to-day the department is carrying on thousands of investigations which go back twenty or thirty years. Anyone who has purchased a business in the meantime may be liable to pay income tax.
I suggest that the hon. member discuss the matter with the commissioner of income tax. It is a little difficult for me to discuss it without knowing the case to which he refers.
Could we hear a little of the interesting conversation that is going on over there? Things have been rather tiring and we should like to hear the interesting conversation on this private transaction.
I am sorry. I was not saying much except that it was pretty hard to give an answer to the hon. gentleman unless I knew the particular case.
It was an individual case, was it not, not a question of principle?
It is not an individual case when thousands of investigations are going on at the present time throughout Canada.

It sounded like it.
Mr. O'NEILL: I believe the income tax is one of the fairest taxes that we have in Canada because it is collected from people who are best able to pay. In my opinion one of the great troubles is that too much of the wealth is in too few hands. This schedule of income taxes goes up one per cent per $1,000 until 18 per cent is reached, and then it refers one to chapter 41 for the taxes on the higher incomes. If the schedule is correct that far, why should there be any change? If it is not correct in the lower brackets, why not change the income tax set-up and have it right from the start? The increase in taxation should continue right from the start. In other words, when you reach a certain income there should be 100 per cent tax.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Does the item carry?
Mr. O'NEILL: Is that an unreasonable or unfair question?

I did not know the hon. gentleman was asking a question; I thought he was making a suggestion. I can tell him that there are persons in Canada who, if they were situated in a certain way, would have to pay the whole of their income in taxes.
Mr. O'NEILL: What amount of income is that?

Is that not a question which should be asked privately?
Mr. O'NEILL: I am sorry if I asked an unfair question or a question which should not be asked here. It seems to me that if this schedule is right at the start there is no reason why it should not continue right along from there. If the schedule is wrong at the start, it should be corrected. There should be no difference between the low paid man and the high paid man.
Is any information available as to the income taxes paid by any group of taxpayers according to the size of their incomes?

Will the hon. gentleman allow that question to stand?
Item stands.
Progress reported.
